_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning to choose the best type of display for our data and justify our choices.

toLevel2.question: A bar chart is used for categorical data, while a histogram is used for continuous numerical data.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Bar charts display discrete categories, while histograms display continuous data grouped into intervals.

distractors.explanation: Confuses the data types suitable for each display.

toLevel2.question: A pie chart is the best choice when you have more than ten categories to display.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Pie charts become cluttered and hard to read with many categories. A bar chart is better for ten or more categories.

distractors.explanation: Ignores that too many slices make pie charts unreadable.

toLevel2.question: A scatter plot is used to show the relationship between two numerical variables.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Scatter plots plot pairs of values on x and y axes to reveal patterns, trends and correlations.

distractors.explanation: Confuses scatter plots with other display types.

toLevel2.question: A box plot displays every individual data value in the dataset.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Box plots summarise data using five statistics (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and do not show individual values.

distractors.explanation: Confuses box plots with stem-and-leaf plots, which do show individual values.

toLevel2.question: A line graph is appropriate for comparing quantities across separate categories such as favourite sports.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Categories are discrete; a line graph implies continuity between points. A bar chart is more appropriate for separate categories.

distractors.explanation: Confuses categorical comparison with time-series trends.

toLevel2.question: A histogram is the correct display for showing favourite colours chosen by students.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Favourite colours are categorical data, which should be shown using a bar chart, not a histogram.

distractors.explanation: Confuses categorical data with continuous numerical data.

toLevel2.question: A stem-and-leaf plot preserves all the original data values in the dataset.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Each leaf represents an individual value, so the full dataset can be reconstructed from the plot.

distractors.explanation: Confuses stem-and-leaf plots with histograms, which group data.

toLevel2.question: A dot plot is only useful for datasets with more than 500 values.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Dot plots work best for small to moderate datasets. Large datasets make dot plots cluttered.

distractors.explanation: Reverses the suitability; dot plots are better for smaller datasets.

toLevel2.question: Box plots are useful for comparing the spread of data across multiple groups.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Side-by-side box plots show median, quartiles and range for each group, making spread comparison straightforward.

distractors.explanation: Ignores that box plots are specifically designed for group comparisons.

toLevel2.question: Any type of data display can be used for any type of data without affecting interpretation.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Different displays suit different data types. Using the wrong display can mislead or obscure important features.

distractors.explanation: Ignores that mismatched displays can distort understanding.

toLevel2.question: A pie chart shows how parts contribute to a whole, with all slices adding up to 100%.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Pie charts represent proportions of a total, with all slices summing to 100%.

distractors.explanation: Misunderstands the fundamental structure of pie charts.

toLevel2.question: When comparing two groups, a single pie chart can display both distributions side by side.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A pie chart shows only one group's proportions. Comparing two groups requires two separate pie charts or a different display type.

distractors.explanation: Assumes a single pie chart can show multiple groups, which it cannot.

toLevel2.question: Which display is best for showing how a student's test scores changed over a school term?
toLevel2.correct: A line graph with time on the horizontal axis
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Line graphs connect data points over time, clearly showing upward or downward trends.

distractors.answer: A pie chart showing each test result as a slice
distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions, not trends over time.

distractors.answer: A single box plot of all scores combined together
distractors.explanation: A box plot summarises all scores but hides the time order.

distractors.answer: A Venn diagram comparing high and low test scores
distractors.explanation: Venn diagrams show set overlaps, not numerical trends.

toLevel2.question: A student wants to display the proportion of students who prefer each of four sports. Which display should they use?
toLevel2.correct: A pie chart or a bar chart
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Both pie charts and bar charts effectively show proportions across a small number of categories.

distractors.answer: A histogram with equal interval widths
distractors.explanation: Histograms are for continuous data, not categories.

distractors.answer: A scatter plot with two numerical axes
distractors.explanation: Scatter plots show relationships between two numerical variables, not categories.

distractors.answer: A stem-and-leaf plot of sport preferences
distractors.explanation: Stem-and-leaf plots are for numerical data, not categorical preferences.

toLevel2.question: Which display type groups continuous data into intervals?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Histograms divide continuous data into equal-width intervals and show frequency per interval.

distractors.explanation: Bar charts display separate categories, not grouped intervals.
Pie charts show proportions of a whole, not interval-grouped data.
Scatter plots display individual data pairs, not grouped intervals.

toLevel2.question: When is a box plot most useful?
toLevel2.correct: When comparing the spread and centre of multiple groups
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Box plots clearly show median, quartiles and range, making group comparisons efficient.

distractors.answer: When showing how data changes over time in a series
distractors.explanation: Time-series data is better shown with a line graph.

distractors.answer: When displaying the proportion of each category overall
distractors.explanation: Proportions of categories are shown with pie or bar charts.

distractors.answer: When every individual data value needs to be visible
distractors.explanation: Box plots hide individual values; stem-and-leaf or dot plots show them.

toLevel2.question: What type of data does a scatter plot require?
toLevel2.correct: Two numerical variables measured on the same individuals
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Scatter plots need paired numerical data, one for each axis, from the same subjects.

distractors.answer: One categorical variable with multiple response options
distractors.explanation: Categorical data is shown with bar or pie charts, not scatter plots.

distractors.answer: A single numerical variable measured once for each case
distractors.explanation: One variable is shown with a histogram or dot plot, not a scatter plot.

distractors.answer: Two categorical variables with no numerical component
distractors.explanation: Two categorical variables require a two-way table, not a scatter plot.

toLevel2.question: Which display would be least appropriate for showing the distribution of heights of 30 students?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Heights are continuous numerical data. Pie charts are designed for categorical proportions, not continuous distributions.

distractors.explanation: Histograms are ideal for showing the distribution of continuous numerical data.
Stem-and-leaf plots work well for 30 numerical values.
Dot plots can effectively display 30 numerical values.

toLevel2.question: Why do bar charts have gaps between bars while histograms do not?
toLevel2.correct: Bar chart categories are separate; histogram intervals are continuous
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Gaps in bar charts show that categories are distinct. Touching histogram bars show continuous, unbroken intervals.

distractors.answer: Bar charts are drawn incorrectly whenever any gaps are included between the bars
distractors.explanation: Gaps are a standard and intentional feature of bar charts.

distractors.answer: Histograms always use wider bars than bar charts do
distractors.explanation: Bar width varies; the presence or absence of gaps relates to data type.

distractors.answer: The gap size in bar charts represents the data range
distractors.explanation: Gaps do not represent any data value; they visually separate categories.

toLevel2.question: A student wants to show whether there is a link between hours of sleep and exam marks. Which display should they choose?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Scatter plots display the relationship between two numerical variables, revealing patterns or correlations.

distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions of one variable, not relationships between two.
Bar charts are for categorical data, not two continuous numerical variables.
A histogram shows the distribution of one variable, not the relationship between two.

toLevel2.question: Which display is best for comparing distributions of two small datasets while preserving all individual values?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots show all individual values for two groups with a shared stem.

distractors.answer: Two separate pie charts of each dataset
distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions, not individual numerical values.

distractors.answer: A single histogram combining all data values
distractors.explanation: Combining data hides group differences.

distractors.answer: A scatter plot of both datasets on one graph
distractors.explanation: Scatter plots require paired variables, not group comparisons.

toLevel2.question: What is a key advantage of using a dot plot over a histogram?
toLevel2.correct: Each individual data value is visible as a separate dot
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Dot plots place one dot per value, making it easy to count exact values and spot clusters.

distractors.answer: Dot plots can display categorical data more effectively
distractors.explanation: Dot plots are for numerical data, not categorical data.

distractors.answer: Dot plots always have more bars than a histogram does
distractors.explanation: Dot plots use dots, not bars; the comparison does not apply.

distractors.answer: Dot plots automatically calculate the mean and median
distractors.explanation: Dot plots display data visually; they do not compute statistics.

toLevel2.question: A teacher wants to show how the class budget is divided among five expense categories. Which display is most appropriate?
toLevel2.correct: A pie chart showing each category as a proportion
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A pie chart clearly shows how parts make up a whole, ideal for budget breakdowns with few categories.

distractors.answer: A histogram of expense amounts across intervals
distractors.explanation: Histograms show distributions, not parts of a whole.

distractors.answer: A scatter plot comparing categories to amounts spent
distractors.explanation: Scatter plots need two numerical variables, not categories.

distractors.answer: A stem-and-leaf plot of all expense dollar values
distractors.explanation: Stem-and-leaf plots show numerical distributions, not category proportions.

toLevel2.question: When should a researcher choose a histogram over a stem-and-leaf plot?
toLevel2.correct: When the dataset is large and individual values are not needed
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Histograms efficiently summarise large datasets by grouping values into intervals.

distractors.answer: When the dataset has fewer than ten observations in total
distractors.explanation: Very small datasets are better shown with stem-and-leaf or dot plots.

distractors.answer: When every individual data value must remain visible
distractors.explanation: Stem-and-leaf plots preserve individual values; histograms do not.

distractors.answer: When the data contains only categorical non-numerical values
distractors.explanation: Neither display is suitable for categorical data; a bar chart should be used.

toLevel2.sentence: A {{blank:1}} chart shows proportions of a whole, while a {{blank:2}} chart compares quantities across separate categories.

blanks.correctExplanation: Pie charts display how parts contribute to a total, with slices adding to 100%.

distractors.explanation: Bar charts compare quantities across categories, not proportions of a whole.
Line charts show trends over time, not part-of-whole relationships.

blanks.correctExplanation: Bar charts use bar heights to compare values across distinct categories.

distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions, not direct quantity comparisons.
Scatter plots show relationships between two numerical variables.

toLevel2.sentence: A {{blank:1}} plot is used to explore the relationship between two {{blank:2}} variables.

blanks.correctExplanation: Scatter plots place paired values on x and y axes to reveal patterns.

distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions, not variable relationships.
Box plots summarise one variable's distribution, not bivariate relationships.

blanks.correctExplanation: Scatter plots require two numerical (quantitative) variables for the axes.

distractors.explanation: Categorical variables cannot be plotted on scatter plot axes.
Ordinal data can sometimes be plotted but scatter plots are designed for truly numerical data.

toLevel3.question: A histogram is always a better choice than a box plot for comparing the distributions of five groups.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Five histograms are hard to compare visually. Side-by-side box plots make five-group comparisons much clearer.

distractors.explanation: Ignores that multiple histograms are harder to compare than parallel box plots.

toLevel3.question: A scatter plot can prove that one variable directly causes changes in another variable.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Scatter plots show association, not causation. Confounding variables may explain the observed pattern.

distractors.explanation: Confuses correlation with causation.

toLevel3.question: Choosing a display type is purely a matter of personal preference with no effect on the message conveyed.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Different displays emphasise different features. A poorly chosen display can obscure patterns or mislead the audience.

distractors.explanation: Ignores that display choice affects what the audience sees and interprets.

toLevel3.question: A pie chart can mislead if the slices do not add up to 100% of the total.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Pie charts must represent a complete whole. If categories overlap or are incomplete, the chart is misleading.

distractors.explanation: Assumes pie charts always work, ignoring that incomplete data distorts the display.

toLevel3.question: A bar chart and a histogram are interchangeable because both use rectangular bars.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Bar charts are for categorical data with gaps between bars. Histograms are for continuous data with touching bars. Their purposes differ.

distractors.explanation: Focuses only on the visual similarity of bars while ignoring the different data types.

toLevel3.question: When a dataset is very large, a box plot can summarise its key features more efficiently than a stem-and-leaf plot.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Box plots condense data into five key statistics, making them ideal for summarising large datasets compactly.

distractors.explanation: Ignores that listing thousands of leaves in a stem-and-leaf plot is impractical.

toLevel3.question: A line graph is appropriate for displaying student enrolment numbers at a school across five different subjects.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Subjects are categories, not a continuous time sequence. A bar chart is more appropriate for comparing enrolment across subjects.

distractors.explanation: Confuses categorical comparisons with time-series trends.

toLevel3.question: Side-by-side box plots are effective for comparing the medians and spreads of multiple groups.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Box plots clearly display the median, interquartile range and overall range, making multi-group comparison straightforward.

distractors.explanation: Fails to recognise the comparative strength of parallel box plots.

toLevel3.question: A student has data on the amount of rainfall each day for a month. They want to show how rainfall is distributed. Which display is most appropriate?
toLevel3.correct: A histogram showing frequency across rainfall intervals
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Daily rainfall is continuous numerical data, making a histogram the ideal choice for showing distribution shape.

distractors.answer: A pie chart showing each day as a percentage of total rain
distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions; 30 slices would be cluttered and unhelpful.

distractors.answer: A bar chart with one bar for each amount of rainfall
distractors.explanation: Continuous data should be grouped into intervals, not treated as separate categories.

distractors.answer: A scatter plot with no second variable to compare
distractors.explanation: Scatter plots need two variables; a single-variable distribution uses histograms.

toLevel3.question: A researcher wants to compare the distributions of exam scores for three different classes. Which display allows the most efficient comparison?
toLevel3.correct: Side-by-side box plots for each class
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Box plots placed side by side show median, spread and outliers for all three classes at a glance.

distractors.answer: Three separate pie charts of each class's scores
distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions, not score distributions.

distractors.answer: A single histogram combining all three classes
distractors.explanation: Combining data hides differences between the classes.

distractors.answer: A scatter plot of class number versus score
distractors.explanation: Class number is categorical, not suitable as a scatter plot axis.

toLevel3.question: A council collects data on the type of transport residents use to get to work (car, bus, train, bicycle, walking). What display best shows the relative popularity of each mode?
toLevel3.correct: A bar chart with transport modes on the horizontal axis
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Transport mode is categorical data, and a bar chart clearly compares frequencies across categories.

distractors.answer: A histogram with transport modes grouped into intervals
distractors.explanation: Transport modes cannot be grouped into numerical intervals.

distractors.answer: A scatter plot comparing transport mode to distance
distractors.explanation: The question asks about mode popularity, not the relationship with distance.

distractors.answer: A stem-and-leaf plot listing all transport choices
distractors.explanation: Stem-and-leaf plots are for numerical data, not categorical choices.

toLevel3.question: A scientist records the temperature at the same location every hour for a week. Which display best shows the temperature trend?
toLevel3.correct: A line graph with time on the horizontal axis
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Line graphs connect data points over time, making hourly trends and patterns clearly visible.

distractors.answer: A pie chart showing temperature proportions per day
distractors.explanation: Temperature readings are not parts of a whole.

distractors.answer: A bar chart with one bar per temperature reading
distractors.explanation: 168 individual bars would be cluttered and miss the time-trend pattern.

distractors.answer: A box plot summarising all 168 temperature readings
distractors.explanation: A box plot hides the temporal pattern, showing only summary statistics.

toLevel3.question: Why might a researcher choose a box plot over a histogram to display their data?
toLevel3.correct: To efficiently compare multiple groups on a single display
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Box plots are compact enough to place several side by side, making multi-group comparison straightforward.

distractors.answer: To display every individual data value in the dataset
distractors.explanation: Box plots hide individual values; dot or stem-and-leaf plots show them.

distractors.answer: To show the exact shape of the distribution in fine detail
distractors.explanation: Histograms show shape in more detail than box plots do.

distractors.answer: To display the proportion of each category as a percentage
distractors.explanation: Proportions are shown with pie charts, not box plots.

toLevel3.question: A student has paired data: each student's height and shoe size. Which display would reveal whether taller students tend to have larger shoes?
toLevel3.correct: A scatter plot with height and shoe size on the axes
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Scatter plots reveal relationships between paired numerical variables, showing patterns like positive correlation.

distractors.answer: Two separate histograms of heights and of shoe sizes independently
distractors.explanation: Separate histograms do not show the relationship between the two variables.

distractors.answer: A pie chart showing proportions of each shoe size category
distractors.explanation: Pie charts cannot show the height-shoe size relationship.

distractors.answer: A single box plot of heights for the entire class group
distractors.explanation: A single box plot ignores shoe sizes and shows only the height distribution.

toLevel3.question: A newspaper shows a pie chart of 'favourite ice cream flavours' with 15 different slices. What is a valid criticism of this display choice?
toLevel3.correct: Too many slices make the chart hard to read and compare
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Fifteen slices create tiny, hard-to-distinguish segments. A bar chart would allow easier comparison.

distractors.answer: Pie charts can never display food preference data
distractors.explanation: Pie charts can show preferences; the issue is the number of categories.

distractors.answer: The chart would work better with even more slices added
distractors.explanation: More slices would worsen the readability problem, not improve it.

distractors.answer: Ice cream flavours can only be shown using histograms
distractors.explanation: Flavours are categorical; histograms are for continuous numerical data.

toLevel3.question: A student argues that 'any display is fine as long as the data is correct.' What is wrong with this reasoning?
toLevel3.correct: The display choice affects what features the audience can see and understand
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A poorly chosen display can hide important patterns or suggest false ones, even with correct data.

distractors.answer: The student is completely correct because data accuracy is all that matters
distractors.explanation: Accuracy is necessary but not sufficient; display choice affects interpretation.

distractors.answer: Only histograms are valid for any type of data that is collected
distractors.explanation: Histograms are not suitable for all data types, such as categorical data.

distractors.answer: Data can never be displayed correctly in any visual format at all
distractors.explanation: Many displays effectively communicate data when chosen appropriately.

toLevel3.question: When comparing the spread of test scores across four year levels, which display would best allow the audience to see medians, quartiles and outliers for each group at a glance?
toLevel3.correct: Four side-by-side box plots
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Box plots are specifically designed to compare centre, spread and outliers across multiple groups.

distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions, not numerical distributions.
Combining data from four groups hides individual group differences.
A line graph would only show means or medians, not the full distribution.

toLevel3.question: A data analyst has 12 monthly sales figures. They want to show both the individual values and the trend over the year. Which combination of displays would work best?
toLevel3.correct: A line graph to show the trend with data points marked
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A line graph with marked data points shows both the individual monthly values and the overall trend direction.

distractors.answer: A pie chart showing each month as a proportion of total sales
distractors.explanation: Pie charts hide the time trend and cannot show monthly progression.

distractors.answer: A histogram grouping the 12 values into intervals of revenue
distractors.explanation: Histograms lose the time order and cannot show trends.

distractors.answer: A scatter plot of month number versus nothing else at all
distractors.explanation: A scatter plot needs two variables; plotting one against nothing is invalid.

toLevel3.question: Why is a stem-and-leaf plot preferred over a histogram when the dataset has only 15 values?
toLevel3.correct: It preserves all 15 individual values while still showing distribution shape
toLevel3.correctExplanation: With only 15 values, listing every leaf is practical and retains detail that a histogram would lose.

distractors.answer: Histograms cannot display datasets with fewer than 50 values
distractors.explanation: Histograms can display any size, but they are less informative for small datasets.

distractors.answer: Stem-and-leaf plots automatically sort data alphabetically
distractors.explanation: Stem-and-leaf plots sort data numerically, not alphabetically.

distractors.answer: Histograms always require a computer while stem-and-leaf plots do not
distractors.explanation: Both can be drawn by hand or with technology.

toLevel3.question: A student displays categorical survey results using a histogram instead of a bar chart. What error have they made?
toLevel3.correct: They used a continuous-data display for discrete categorical data
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Histograms are for continuous numerical data with touching bars. Categorical data requires a bar chart with gaps.

distractors.answer: There is no error because histograms work for all data types
distractors.explanation: Histograms are specifically for continuous data; using them for categories misleads.

distractors.answer: The error is that the bars should have been horizontal instead
distractors.explanation: Bar orientation is a style choice; the real issue is using the wrong display type.

distractors.answer: Surveys can never be displayed using any kind of chart or graph
distractors.explanation: Survey results can be effectively displayed with appropriate chart choices.

toLevel3.sentence: A {{blank:1}} graph is best for showing how data changes over {{blank:2}}, connecting each data point in sequence.

blanks.correctExplanation: Line graphs connect points in chronological order, revealing trends and patterns.

distractors.explanation: Bar charts compare categories; they do not connect points over time.
Pie charts show proportions at one point in time, not changes over time.

blanks.correctExplanation: The horizontal axis typically represents time in a line graph showing trends.

distractors.explanation: Categories are compared using bar charts, not line graphs.

toLevel3.sentence: A pie chart is appropriate when showing how {{blank:1}} make up a {{blank:2}}, with all slices totalling 100%.

blanks.correctExplanation: Pie charts show how individual categories contribute to the total.

distractors.explanation: Trends are shown with line graphs, not pie charts.
Paired data relationships are shown with scatter plots.

blanks.correctExplanation: All slices represent portions of a complete total that sums to 100%.

distractors.explanation: Pie charts show composition at one point, not trends over time.
Paired relationships are explored with scatter plots, not pie charts.

toLevel3.sentence: A dot plot works well for {{blank:1}} datasets because each individual value is represented by a single {{blank:2}}.

blanks.correctExplanation: Dot plots become cluttered with too many values; they are best for smaller datasets.

distractors.explanation: Large datasets produce overcrowded dot plots that are hard to read.
Dot plots are for numerical data; categorical data uses bar charts.

blanks.correctExplanation: Each observation appears as one dot, preserving individual data values.

distractors.explanation: Bars are used in bar charts and histograms, not dot plots.
Slices are used in pie charts, not dot plots.

toLevel3.sentence: Choosing an inappropriate display can {{blank:1}} important patterns or create {{blank:2}} impressions of the data.

blanks.correctExplanation: A wrong display type may not reveal key features like skewness, bimodality or outliers.

distractors.explanation: Inappropriate displays hide real patterns rather than creating new ones.
Wrong displays make understanding worse, not better.

blanks.correctExplanation: An inappropriate display can suggest patterns that do not exist or hide those that do.

distractors.explanation: Inappropriate displays create inaccuracy, not accuracy.

toLevel4.question: A scatter plot with a clear upward trend proves that one variable causes the other to increase.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Scatter plots show association, not causation. A trend may be due to confounding variables or coincidence.

distractors.explanation: Confuses correlation with causation.

toLevel4.question: When the audience needs to compare exact values across groups, a bar chart is usually more effective than a pie chart.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Bar heights are easier to compare precisely than pie slice angles, especially with similar-sized categories.

distractors.explanation: Ignores that humans are better at comparing lengths than angles.

toLevel4.question: A student presents a scatter plot of ice cream sales versus drowning incidents and claims ice cream causes drownings. Evaluate this conclusion.
toLevel4.correct: The correlation is likely due to a confounding variable such as hot weather
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Hot weather increases both ice cream sales and swimming, creating a spurious correlation.

distractors.answer: The scatter plot proves the causal link between the two variables
distractors.explanation: Scatter plots show association, not causation.

distractors.answer: The student should have used a pie chart to show causation clearly
distractors.explanation: No display type can establish causation from observational data.

distractors.answer: Ice cream data and drowning data can never be plotted together
distractors.explanation: Any two numerical variables can be plotted; the issue is interpretation, not the plot.

toLevel4.question: A school wants to compare the distribution of reading test scores across Year 7, 8, 9 and 10 and present the results at assembly. Which display is most efficient for this purpose?
toLevel4.correct: Four side-by-side box plots on one graph
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Box plots compactly show median, spread and outliers, allowing quick four-way comparison.

distractors.answer: Four separate histograms on different slides in a presentation
distractors.explanation: Separate slides make direct comparison difficult for the audience.

distractors.answer: A single pie chart combining all four year levels into one
distractors.explanation: Pie charts show proportions, not score distributions.

distractors.answer: A table listing every individual student's score by year level
distractors.explanation: Raw data tables are overwhelming for assembly audiences.

toLevel4.question: A real estate company presents a bar chart of median house prices across suburbs. A competitor presents the same data as a pie chart. Which display better serves the audience trying to compare suburb prices?
toLevel4.correct: The bar chart, because bar heights allow direct comparison of prices
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Bar charts make it easy to compare specific values across categories. Pie charts show proportions, which is less useful here.

distractors.answer: The pie chart, because it shows each suburb's share of the total
distractors.explanation: Share of total is less useful than comparing actual median prices.

distractors.answer: Both are equally effective for comparing suburb house prices
distractors.explanation: Bar charts are superior for comparing quantities across many categories.

distractors.answer: Neither is appropriate because house prices require scatter plots
distractors.explanation: Scatter plots compare two variables; here we compare one variable across categories.

toLevel4.question: A researcher has data on the heights and weights of 200 students. They want to (a) compare height distributions across genders and (b) explore the height-weight relationship. Which combination of displays addresses both goals?
toLevel4.correct: Box plots for gender comparison and a scatter plot for the height-weight relationship
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Box plots compare distributions across categories, while scatter plots reveal bivariate relationships.

distractors.answer: Two pie charts and a bar chart for both analyses
distractors.explanation: Pie charts cannot show numerical distributions or bivariate relationships.

distractors.answer: A single histogram that includes both height and weight data
distractors.explanation: One histogram can only show one variable's distribution.
